title: Transmitting the News From Neptune: Carl Estabrook’s Embrace of the Life Force
author: Jeffrey St. Clair
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/carlestabrook.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/22/transmitting-
the-news-from-neptune-carl-estabrooks-embrace-of-the-life-force/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/carlestabrook.png)

Carl Estabrook delivering the News From Neptune from the studio in Urbana,
Illinois.

When I think of my friend Carl Estabrook, as I often have in the weeks since
he died, I see someone who was fully engaged with life. Almost every aspect of
life mattered to Carl, was worthy of being experienced, observed, analyzed,
discussed and debated. He had a roving mind and an unchained spirit. There was
nothing dour about him. He was witty and charming and empathetic. He also knew
who the enemies of life were, the people and institutions who profited from
inflicting pain on others and he didn’t hesitate to call them out. In other
words, he had the courage of his conscience. He put what he believed into
practice.

Carl spoke his mind. He believed everyone should and defended their right to
do so, whatever they said. Speaking his mind often got Carl in trouble, as it
tends to do when you speak your mind about the things that really matter in
life: politics, art, education, war, capitalism and religion. So his stints at
the universities where he taught tended to be fractious and abbreviated: Notre
Dame, Brown, Rochester, Stonehill and Illinois. Still, he left his mark at all
of them. The best teachers I’ve had challenged both their students and their
colleagues and administrators. Carl was one of them. I didn’t take any of his
classes, but I learned from his writing, his public speeches, debates, and
private chats. He taught me how to see old disputes in new ways. His analysis
pierced through the corrupting cant of political speech to the core truths
hidden beneath.

Carl saw through both political parties, but he didn’t give up on politics as
a means of organizing people to make their lives better. No matter how bleak
the circumstances, he didn’t surrender to fatalism. He admired Ralph Nader and
Jesse Jackson’s campaigns and saw the value, when many progressives couldn’t,
in Ron Paul’s anti-war crusades. In 2004, Carl ran for Congress as a Green and
garnered a respectable four percent of the vote. Four years later, having seen
Obama up close in Illinois, he didn’t fall for the hope and change rhetoric
and he soon became one of the most astute and acerbic critics of Obama’s
dismal presidency. Carl was certainly not surprised at Obama’s rapid
transformation from anti-war Constitutional lawyer into a president who
authorized warrantless drone hits against American citizens and their
families. Yesterday’s preachy defenders of the Bill of Rights often invoke the
powers of the police state once in office.

He was a free speech absolutist. He went so far as to defend the Supreme
Court’s Citizens United decision on First Amendment grounds. I disagreed with
him vehemently, but I knew there was a consistency to Carl’s argument, that it
was well-reasoned, logical, even irrefutable within his frame of moral
reference. When CounterPunch was caught up in the RussiaGate hysteria for
publishing a few pieces by someone under the pen name “Alice Donovan,” Carl’s
advice was adamant: “Don’t back down. Don’t apologize. Publish whomever and
whatever you want. It’s none of their business.” If I’d taken it, I’d probably
saved ourselves a lot of unnecessary trouble and distraction.

Carl was a militant civil libertarian who abhorred bigotry in all of its
guises, especially towards outsider sects often despised by liberals. He
enjoyed puncturing the hypocrisy of censors and cultural scolds and once
defended a polygamist Mormon community against media and legal persecution
with such vigor I was tempted to write an amicus brief in their defense.

Three key people shaped Carl’s thinking and he thought deeply about almost
everything, including the ups-and-downs of the NFL team in Washington–the
Catholic philosopher and theologian Herbert McCabe, Noam Chomsky and his wife
of 62 years, Leigh, the former dean of the University of Illinois’ School of
Information Sciences. By one of those strange twists of fate that Thomas
Pynchon called a Kute Korrespondance, my wife, Kimberly, was one of Leigh’s
graduate students, though it took a while for any of us to realize the
connection.

Carl took his Catholicism seriously, in the same way the Catholic Workers and
Liberation Theologians did. He wanted his church to live up to its ideals. He
certainly did. Carl was pro-life, which meant that he was anti-war, against
the death penalty and anti-abortion. He ministered to the poor, the hungry and
the abandoned. His views on abortion conflicted with mine and alienated some
of his political and academic allies. But it was honestly held and consistent
with the philosophy by which he lived his life. Carl explained his positions
clearly and firmly, which is all you can ask for and more than you usually
get.

Carl’s weekly political radio show was called the News from Neptune. The title
was a tribute to Chomsky, whose method of political analysis the columnist
Jeff Greenfield had once derisively described as coming from “Planet Neptune.”
The news may sound like it’s coming from Neptune, but it accurately described
the corrupted state of the American Empire in late capitalism. I was happy to
publish Carl’s political writings under the same banner on
[CounterPunch](https://www.counterpunch.org/author/gu5r5ch111/) for many
years. The analysis was sharp and fresh and to the point. Carl was a
contrarian, but not in the performative sense of Christopher Hitchens, which
led him to help plot bombing raids in the Bush Executive Office Building.
Carl’s contrariness cut through political propaganda to get you closer to the
reality of what was really going on. He often got you uncomfortably close,
which is what the best political analysis and journalism must do, especially
in times of economic privation, forever wars and state terror.

Carl was an actor in a local theater company where he played Prospero in “The
Tempest,” a play written by Edward de Vere, the Earl of Oxford, or so he
argued with vigor and good humor. I’m a Marlowe man, myself and we had fun
debating the relative merits of both as the real author of the plays
attributed to the Bard of Stratford, neither of us giving an inch of ground.
He deeply admired the writing of Samuel Beckett, especially Beckett’s plays,
and I consulted him on my parody of Endgame, which serves as the concluding
chapter of my book on Bernie Sanders.

He read widely and voraciously: history, philosophy, theology, psychology,
drama, poetry, novels. There was rarely a book I’d read that Carl hadn’t. I
tried to take him by surprise, but rarely succeeded. More often he was
introducing me to books and writers I hadn’t read. His belief in the power and
potency of poems and poets was such that he co-hosted a weekly poetry radio
show, which he lured me into appearing on a couple of times. I remember
reciting and mangling the meter of Keats’s magnificent poem “To Autumn,”
followed by a lively discussion about its radical subtext as a critique of the
anti-gleaning laws enacted by the landed British gentry. I quickly found he
knew more about those grim episodes of English history than I did. So I sat
back, listened and learned.

In our last email conversation, a few weeks before he died, Carl asked what
I’d been reading for fun and I told him I’d spent the last four months reading
Proust’s In Search of Lost Time, if not for fun, then out of obligation, since
Proust had spent the time to write. Carl replied: “As I lack your industry, I
will probably leave Proust forever unread: but you’re an encouragement to do
otherwise… I will at least get back to reading all the manifestations of
CounterPunch.” That’s a friend, a friend I'll deeply miss.

Now, a couple of weeks after his passing, I come back to the fearless
engagement Carl had with life: embracing its preciousness, defending its
vitality among the weak, the infirm, the marginalized and dispossessed among
us. Seeing each life as inviolate as any other was the essence of Carl’s life
work. It’s the way he lived. The way he treated and cared for his family, his
friends, his colleagues, his neighbors and fellow parishioners. When I think
of Carl today, I’m reminded of a poem by DH Lawrence called “We Are the
Transmitters,” where Lawrence writes: “And if, as we work, we can transmit
life into our work, life, still more life, rushes into us to compensate, to be
ready and we ripple with life through the days.” The ripples of Carl
Estabrook’s life don’t stop with him; they carry on, they continue to
transmit…
